'''Catherine L. Craig'''<ref name="GF"/> (born February 2, 1951) is an American zoologist and conservationist. She is a 1995 [[Guggenheim Fellow]] and is founder of Conservation through Poverty Alleviation International.
==Biography==
Craig was born on February 2, 1951, in [[Oxnard, California]],<ref name="GF"/> and raised on a citrus farm in [[Ventura, California|Ventura]].<ref name="Baker 2008"/> While studying at [[Stanford University]], Craig studied chimpanzee ethology at [[Gombe Stream National Park]] for six months starting in 1972, working alongside [[Jane Goodall]]; her experience there inspired her to study silk, seeing it as a way for people to protect habitats with limited financial options.<ref name="mongabay"/><ref name="Baker 2008"/> She obtained a BA in human biology from Stanford in 1973, and later a MS in zoology from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1976.<ref name="mongabay"/><ref name="Baker 2008"/> 

In 1985, Craig obtained a PhD from [[Cornell University]];<ref name="GF"/> her doctoral dissertation ''Predator-Prey Dynamics: The Role of Spider and Insect Ecological and Behavioral Interactions in the Evolution of the Araneoidea'' was supervised by [[Simon A. Levin]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catherine Craig |url=https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=67455 |access-date=2026-10-01 |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project}}</ref> She became an assistant professor of biology at [[Yale University]] in 1985, before being promoted to associate professor in 1991.<ref name="GF"/>  By 1990, she had made several visits to Panama as part of scientific studies funded by the [[National Geographic Society]], [[National Science Foundation]], and the [[Smithsonian Institution]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Jarvis |first=Elena |date=1990-07-22 |title=Spiders, Creatures of mystery |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/934292643/ |work=Ventura County Star |page=B-1 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

Craig studied wild silk throughout Asia and Africa, before selecting Madagascar for its biodiversity and high poverty.<ref name="mongabay"/> In 2003, she founded Conservation through Poverty Alleviation International (CPALI),<ref name="Baker 2008"/> an NGO meant to build an economy on silk through training, tree planting, and plant finding, though it encountered challenges such as shipping costs, resource constraints, and other logistical issues.<ref name="mongabay"/> She then started fieldwork on that country in 2004, centering on farmers at border forests with wild silk caterpillars; this provided a model centered on people's landscapes instead of moving people out.<ref name="mongabay"/> She used a 2007-2008 [[Fulbright Program]] grant to extend the work of CPALI in Madagascar.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catherine Craig {{!}} Fulbright Scholar Program |url=https://fulbrightscholars.org/grantee/catherine-craig |access-date=2026-11-01 |website=fulbrightscholars.org}}</ref>

In 1995,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catherine L. Craig |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/catherine-l-craig/ |access-date=2026-10-01 |website=Guggenheim Fellowships}}</ref> Craig was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] "for a study of silk proteins and the evolution of web-spinning spiders".<ref name="GF">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b4nWAAAAMAAJ |title=Reports of the President and of the Treasurer |publisher=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |year=1996 |page=47-48}}</ref> She was also a 1992 Alfred P. Sloan Foundation Fellow and a 1995-1996 Mary Ingraham Bunting Institute Fellow.<ref name="GF"/> 

She is the author of two books: ''Spider Webs and Silk''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Craig |first=Catherine L. |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Spiderwebs_and_Silk.html?id=PXc8DwAAQBAJ&source=kp_book_description |title=Spiderwebs and Silk: Tracing Evolution From Molecules to Genes to Phenotypes |date=2003-08-21 |publisher=Oxford University Press, USA |isbn=978-0-19-512916-8 |language=en}}</ref> and ''Spider Silk''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brunetta |first=Leslie |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Spider_Silk/JU0w9HVElf8C?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Catherine+Craig+and+Leslie+Brunetta&printsec=frontcover |title=Spider Silk: Evolution and 400 Million Years of Spinning, Waiting, Snagging, and Mating |date=2010-08-23 |publisher=Yale.ORIM |isbn=978-0-300-16315-5 |language=en}}</ref>
